title: About
text: This blog contains posts created for the 2026 St. Lawrence Fellowship. The goal of this fellowship was to visualize in-game win probability in college basketball through data storytelling

title: Frequentist & Bayesian Logistic Regression Models
text: After attaining the final dataset by completing the data collection and data cleaning portions of my project. I’m ready to start the modeling portions of my project. After reading through this research paper, A Bayesian Logistic Regression Framework for In-Game Win Probability Estimation in NCAA Basketball. I realized I should start with a frequentist logistic regression model because I have seen this in my coursework before, and then I can try a bayesian logistic regression model based on what I learned from the research paper.

title: Frequentist & Bayesian Logistic Regression Models
text:
Without Team Rating
Here is how the code for the Frequentist Logistic Regression without Rating model looked:

#log_mod <- glm(home_win ~ time_elapsed + lead_diff + time_elapsed:lead_diff,
 #              data = mbb_pbp_2025, family = "binomial")

I then created the model predictions by using the ggpredict() function from the ggeffects R package, and then I’m able to put them into a plot.

Now with the regression lines we can see the predicted in-game win probability for the home team throughout the game at different lead differences.

title: Frequentist & Bayesian Logistic Regression Models
text:
With Team Rating
Here is how the code for the Frequentist Logistic Regression with Rating model looked:

 #                       time_elapsed:lead_diff + time_elapsed:rating_diff,
  #                    data = final_data, family = "binomial")

This model adds rating_diff and the interaction term between time_elapsed and rating_diff. Now the model is ready to be visualized with a predicted win probability plot that shows how win probability of the home team changes throughout the game.

We can see that the win probability for the home team is shifted __ at the start of the game compared to the previous model. Also we see that both models produce similarly shaped regression lines that are more similar towards the end of the game.

title: MLE & Dynamic Bayes Models
text:
While developing the Frequentist and Bayesian logistic regression models, I also explored a different approach based on the methods presented in Bayesian Estimation of In-Game Home Team Win Probability for College Basketball. Unlike logistic regression, which estimates win probability through a statistical model fitted to predictor variables, these methods estimate win probability directly from historical game outcomes.
The two approaches examined were the Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) method and the Dynamic Bayes method. Both methods use historical combinations of game time and score differential to estimate the probability that the home team will ultimately win. One of the goals of this stage of the project was to determine whether these methods would produce results similar to those reported in the research paper when trained using only a single season of NCAA men’s basketball data.

title: MLE & Dynamic Bayes Models
text:
Using the High-Performance Computing System
A significant part of implementing the Dynamic Bayes method involved learning how to use Ada, St. Lawrence University’s high-performance computer. The computational demands of the model exceeded what was practical on my personal laptop, particularly when working with a full season of second-by-second play-by-play data.
Using the HPC system allowed the model to be executed remotely and run continuously for long periods of time. A full-season Dynamic Bayes run required nearly an entire day of computation, making remote processing essential.
Beyond this project, learning to use an HPC environment was valuable because many modern data science and statistical applications involve datasets or algorithms that are too computationally intensive for a standard laptop. The experience provided an introduction to distributed computing resources and demonstrated how specialized infrastructure can enable analyses that would otherwise be impractical.

title: Data Collection & Initial Exploration
text:
This project was motivated by the question:

How can in-game win probability be estimated and visualized throughout NCAA men’s basketball games to support data-driven storytelling?

The idea emerged from an interest in combining data science and sports, particularly within the context of college basketball. Two research papers provided the foundation for the project. The first, Bayesian Estimation of In-Game Home Team Win Probability for College Basketball, introduced Bayesian approaches that update win probability as a game progresses using information such as score differential and time remaining. The second, A Bayesian Logistic Regression Framework for In-Game Win Probability Estimation in NCAA Basketball, demonstrated how Bayesian logistic regression can be used to estimate real-time win probabilities while incorporating additional game and team-level information.
Together, these papers provided a framework for thinking about how win probability evolves throughout a game. Building on these ideas, the goal of this project was to develop and visualize in-game win probability models using NCAA men’s basketball play-by-play data.

title: Data Collection & Initial Exploration
text:
Data Summary
After gaining familiarity with the raw data, a basic summary was created to better understand the scope of the 2026 season.

#mbb_pbp |> summarise(
 # total_games = n_distinct(game_id),
  #total_playoff_games = n_distinct(game_id[season_type == 3]),
  #total_teams = n_distinct(home_team_id)
  #)

The 2026 dataset contains 6,275 games, including 105 postseason games. These postseason contests extend beyond the NCAA Tournament and include additional tournaments involving teams that did not qualify for March Madness.
The dataset also contains 366 unique home teams and 720 unique away teams. Since there were 365 NCAA Division I men’s basketball programs during the 2026 season, these counts confirm the presence of non-Division I opponents within the data. This observation is consistent with typical scheduling patterns, where Division I programs frequently play exhibition or early-season games against smaller schools.

title: Data Collection & Initial Exploration
text:
Adding Team Ratings
Several of the models developed later in the project incorporated a measure of relative team strength. To capture this information, a variable named rating_diff was created using team ratings obtained from TeamRankings.
These ratings provide a single numerical measure of overall team strength and are updated throughout the season. Because ratings change daily, historical ratings were collected for every date in the season, producing a dataset containing team ratings across time.
Integrating these ratings into the play-by-play data introduced a common data-wrangling challenge of inconsistent team names across sources. ESPN and TeamRankings use different naming conventions for certain schools, including abbreviations and alternate spellings. The fuzzyjoin package was used to resolve many of these mismatched names automatically, while the remaining mismatches were corrected manually.
An additional complication was that TeamRankings only provides ratings for NCAA Division one programs. For non-division one opponents, ratings were assigned as one point below the lowest available division one rating. Once team names were standardized, the ratings dataset was merged with the main play-by-play dataset. Which added the variables home_rating, away_rating, and the derived predictor rating_diff.

title: Predicted Probability Plots
text:
Introduction
With five different models trained on the 2025 season play-by-play data, the next stage of the project focused on visualization. While model performance metrics provide one way to evaluate a win probability model, visualizing predictions throughout an individual game offers a more intuitive way to understand how each model responds to changes in game state.
The primary goal of this stage was to apply the trained models to individual games from the 2026 NCAA men’s basketball season and create predicted win probability plots. These plots track how a team’s probability of winning changes throughout a game and serve as the foundation for the storytelling component of the project.


Finding Case Study Games
Before creating the visualizations, I needed to identify games that would provide interesting case studies. Rather than selecting games with straightforward outcomes, I looked for games that featured large momentum swings, frequent lead changes, or high stakes.
Three games were selected for further analysis:

Duke vs. UConn (Elite Eight) – This NCAA Tournament game featured one of the largest comebacks of the season. Duke built a 19-point lead in the first half before UConn rallied and won on a buzzer-beating three-pointer. This game provided an opportunity to examine how high Duke’s win probability became despite ultimately losing.
Michigan vs. UConn (National Championship) – As the final game of the season, the national championship was a natural case study. Unlike the Duke vs. UConn matchup, this game remained relatively competitive throughout, allowing the models to be evaluated in a different game environment.
Duke vs. Virginia (ACC Championship) – This game featured 16 lead changes, and neither team led by more than seven points. The constant shifts in momentum made it an ideal candidate for examining how win probability responds to a highly competitive game.

An important characteristic to note is that all three games is that they were played at neutral sites. Although the data designate one team as the home team, neither team actually had home-court advantage. This distinction became important when interpreting model predictions and required additional adjustments for some of the methods later in the project.


Creating Predicted Win Probability Plots
To simplify the process of generating visualizations, I created a function that could apply any of the five models to a selected game. Given a game’s play-by-play data and a specified model, the function returned a dataset containing predicted win probabilities at each second of game time.
This approach made it possible to compare models across multiple games without rewriting prediction code for each analysis. Once predictions were generated, they could be visualized using similar plotting code.
The examples below illustrate the types of visualizations produced during this stage of the project.
The first example shows the national championship game between Michigan and UConn using the MLE method.

#ggplot(mich_uconn_mle, aes(x = time_elapsed, y = win_prob)) +
 # geom_line() +
  #geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +
#  geom_vline(xintercept = 1200, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +
 # scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  #labs(x = "Time Elapsed (seconds)",
   #    y = "Predicted Home Win Probability",
    #   title = "Michigan vs UConn - MLE") +
#  theme_minimal()

The second example shows Duke vs. Virginia using the frequentist logistic regression model without team ratings.

#ggplot(duke_va_log, aes(x = time_elapsed, y = win_prob)) +
 # geom_line() +
  #geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +
#  geom_vline(xintercept = 1200, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +
 # scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  #labs(x = "Time Elapsed (seconds)",
   #    y = "Predicted Home Win Probability",
    #   title = "Duke vs Virginia - Logistic w/o Rating") +
#  theme_minimal()

The final example shows Duke vs. UConn using the Bayesian logistic regression model.

#ggplot(duke_uconn_brm, aes(x = time_elapsed, y = win_prob)) +
 # geom_line() +
  #geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +
#  geom_vline(xintercept = 1200, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +
 # scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  #labs(x = "Time Elapsed (seconds)",
   #    y = "Predicted Home Win Probability",
    #   title = "Duke vs UConn - Bayesian Logistic") +
#  theme_minimal()

Although the models differ in how they estimate win probability, the resulting visualizations share a common interpretation. As the score and game situation change, the predicted probability of victory updates continuously. These plots provide a detailed view of momentum shifts and critical turning points that are often lost when looking only at the final score.


Adjusting MLE and Dynamic Bayes for Neutral-Site Games
Lets go back to topic of these games actually being at neutral sites, but one team is denoted as the home team by the data and model. As we saw in the Michigan vs. UConn - MLE predicted probability plot, Michigan’s win probability starts above 50% since they are considered the home team. But when played at a neutral site, and since the MLE method only considered time and score the win probability of both teams should be equal.
Lets use the Michigan vs. UConn game to explain how I fixed this issue. First you assume Michigan as the home team which we already have, when you assume UConn as the home team and you do this by flipping the sign of lead_diff. Then you combine the two different datasets and use this formula to get the win probability of a neutral site game, win_prob_neutral = (win_prob_A + (1 - win_prob_B)) / 2.
The logistic regression models included team strength information through the rating_diff variable, which naturally accounts for differences between teams before the game begins. The MLE and Dynamic Bayes methods, however, rely only on score differential and game time.
As a result, when a team is designated as the home team, these methods assign that team a slight advantage at the start of the game because historically home teams win more often than away teams. For neutral site games, this behavior is unwanted because neither team should have an pre-game advantage before play begins.
This issue was particularly noticeable in the Michigan versus UConn national championship game. When Michigan was treated as the home team, the win probability at the start of the game was greater than 50%, despite the game being played at a neutral site.
To address this issue, each game was evaluated twice. The first version treated Team A as the home team, while the second version treated Team B as the home team by reversing the sign of the score differential. The two resulting probability estimates were then combined into a single neutral-site estimate by averaging the probability for Team A with the complement of Team B’s probability.
This procedure removes the historical home-court advantage embedded within the MLE and Dynamic Bayes methods and ensures that neutral-site games begin at exactly a 50% win probability.
The updated MLE visualization for the Michigan versus UConn national championship game is shown below.

#ggplot(mich_uconn_mle_neutral, aes(x = time_elapsed, y = win_prob_neutral)) +
#  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
 # geom_vline(xintercept = 1200, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +
  #scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 2400, by = 300)) +
#  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
 # labs(title = "Michigan vs UConn MLE Win Probability",
  #     x = "Time Elapsed (seconds)",
   #    y = "Predicted Win Probability (Michigan)") +
#  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

The same adjustment was applied to the Dynamic Bayes method.

#ggplot(duke_uconn_db_neutral, aes(x = time_elapsed, y = win_prob_neutral)) +
 # geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  #geom_vline(xintercept = 1200, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +
#  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 2400, by = 300)) +
 # scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  #labs(title = "Duke vs UConn Dynamic Bayes Win Probability",
   #    x = "Time Elapsed (seconds)",
    #   y = "Predicted Win Probability (Duke)") +
#  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

After the adjustment, both methods produced win probability curves that began at 50% and evolved solely according to the game state. This provided a more appropriate representation of neutral-site postseason games and improved the interpretability of the visualizations.


Conclusion
This post marks the transition from model development to visualization. The trained models were applied to individual games, transforming statistical predictions into win probability plots that illustrate how a team’s chances of winning change throughout a game.
These visualizations reveal aspects of a game that are not captured by the final score alone. Large comebacks, momentum shifts, and critical possessions become visible through changes in predicted win probability, providing a richer view of how games unfold over time.
The next stage of the project focuses on learning the Quarto Closeread extension. These win probability plots become a central component of the storytelling process, allowing statistical analysis and narrative explanation to be combined into an interactive presentation of a basketball game.

title: Learning the Closeread Extension
text:
Introduction
Post 5
Continuing the visualization stage of the project, the next step was learning how to use the Quarto Closeread extension. Closeread is a custom Quarto format that supports scrollytelling, a style of presentation where narrative text and visualizations are linked together as the reader moves through a document.
The goal of this stage was not to analyze basketball games directly, but rather to develop the tools needed to communicate the results of the project effectively. Before creating a final polished presentation, I first needed to understand the features available in Closeread and experiment with different design choices. This process involved building a test document, exploring interactive features, and using custom CSS styling to improve the overall appearance and usability of the final product.


Learning the Closeread Framework
One of the defining features of Closeread is its ability to synchronize text and visualizations. As a reader scrolls through the page, explanatory text appears on one side of the screen while plots, images, or other visual elements remain visible on the other side.
Unlike a traditional report where figures are placed between blocks of text, Closeread allows visualizations to remain fixed while the narrative changes. This structure encourages readers to focus on specific aspects of a plot as they progress through the document and creates a more interactive reading experience.
To learn how this framework operates, I experimented with the core Closeread components, including sections and sticky elements. These features control how text and visualizations are displayed throughout the document and form the foundation of the scrollytelling experience.

The following example demonstrates several of the features that I experimented with while learning the Closeread extension. The win probability plot is included only as a sample visualization and is used to illustrate how narrative text and graphics can interact within a scrollytelling document.





The first feature I explored was the basic Closeread layout. As the reader scrolls through the document, the narrative text changes while the visualization remains fixed on the screen. This creates a stronger connection between the written explanation and the figure being discussed.




Another feature I tested was the ability to zoom into specific regions of a visualization. Using the pan-to and scale-by options, the document can automatically focus on an area of interest. This allows a reader’s attention to be directed toward a specific event or pattern without requiring them to interpret the entire graphic at once. 




The final step is returning to the full visualization. This transition restores the broader context of the plot and allows the reader to connect the highlighted region back to the overall game. When the plot returns to its original view, the picture-in-picture display is no longer needed and disappears automatically.


































Interactive Features and CSS Customization
A major focus of the test document was understanding how Closeread can transform a static visualization into a more interactive experience. The demonstration above illustrates two features that were particularly useful: pan-to and scale-by. Together, these tools allow a document to zoom into selected regions of a figure and direct the reader’s attention toward specific details.
In addition to Closeread’s built-in functionality, I experimented with custom CSS styling to improve the presentation of the document. Initial modifications included adding borders around visualizations, adjusting spacing, and creating colored text containers to improve readability and visual contrast.
The most advanced customization was the picture-in-picture feature displayed during the zoomed view above. When a plot is enlarged, readers can lose sight of the broader context of the visualization. To address this issue, a miniature version of the full plot appears in the corner of the screen while the zoom is active. This allows readers to maintain awareness of where the zoomed region is located within the complete figure. Once the document transitions away from the zoomed section, the miniature plot automatically disappears.


Conclusion
This post documented the process of learning the Quarto Closeread extension and exploring the interactive features that support data-driven storytelling. Through experimentation with scrolling interactions, visualization transitions, and custom CSS styling, I developed a framework for presenting win probability analysis in a more engaging and accessible format.
An important takeaway from this stage of the project was that effective data storytelling requires more than accurate statistical models. While previous stages focused on collecting data, developing models, and generating win probability estimates, this phase emphasized how those results could be communicated to an audience. Features such as guided scrolling, interactive zooming, and custom visual design demonstrated how presentation choices can help readers better understand and engage with statistical analyses.
The following post serves as the culmination of the project. Unlike the previous posts, which focused on methodology, modeling, and development, the final Closeread document is a polished presentation of the 2026 NCAA Men’s Basketball National Championship game. It applies the techniques developed throughout the project to create an interactive narrative centered on the changing win probability throughout the game.
